source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Counting the Legs of Trends and Trading Ranges

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; sides field states mirrored/same

candidates.name: TwoLegMoveTendency
candidates.quote: every trend and every countertrend move has a good chance of breaking down into two legs, and every leg will try to subdivide into two smaller legs.
candidates.description: General context: any move and its correction tend to complete in exactly two legs, recursively at every scale -- the assumption underlying the high 2 / low 2 bar-counting setups and ABC corrections formalized in chapter 17.
candidates.pseudocode: // no new test beyond the leg/pullback counter defined in trends/00_front_matter.json (PullbackLegCounter) and chapter 17's HighLowBarCounter; this candidate records the expectation those primitives encode
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (structural expectation, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: the leg/direction-change criterion is left to the trader's choice, per trends chapter 20's LegDefinition

notes: Same foundational idea as trends/20_two_legs.json's T20-01/T20-02 and trends/00_front_matter.json's T00-19; kept here since this chapter is this book's explicit statement of it.

candidates.name: SubdivisionInTightChannelCaution
candidates.quote: When you are looking for a two-legged move and see one but the two legs are in a relatively tight channel of any kind, such as a wedge, they might in fact be subdivisions of the first leg ... This is especially true if the number of bars in each of the two legs looks inadequate compared to the pattern it is correcting.
candidates.description: If the two apparent legs of a correction sit in a tight channel/wedge and together run fewer bars than a minimum fraction of the pattern they are correcting, treat them as subdivisions of a single first leg rather than a completed two-legged correction, and require a further leg before entering with the trend.
candidates.pseudocode: isTightChannel(correctionBars) && correctionBars < minCorrectionFraction * patternBars -> treatAsSingleLeg (do not yet trade the with-trend entry)

complexity.reason: needs both a channel/tightness test and the bar-span of the pattern being corrected, which requires pivot detection

notes: Brooks gives no numeric fraction; minCorrectionFraction is a reading of 'the number of bars ... looks inadequate.'
Same guideline restated more specifically for wedges in chapter 17's R17-15.

candidates.name: BreakoutTestMeasuredMoveExpectation
candidates.quote: Whenever there is a perfect or near-perfect breakout test, the odds are high that the market will make about a measured move (expect the move up from the bar 12 low to be equal in points to the move from bars 6 to 9).
candidates.description: After a breakout point is retested to within a small tolerance (a 'perfect' breakout test), project a measured-move target equal in size to the leg that preceded the original breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(testLow - breakoutPoint) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize -> target = testLow + (breakoutLegHigh - breakoutLegLow)
candidates.book_order_type: profit-taking limit at the measured-move target

complexity.reason: needs a remembered breakout point and the height of the leg that preceded it, both of which require swing-pivot bookkeeping

notes: Overlaps chapter 8's measured-move/magnet candidates (ranges/08_measured_moves_based_on_gaps_and_trading_ranges.json) and R05-04's breakout-pullback test entry; dedup pass should compare.

candidates.name: FailedDoubleTopFuelsBreakoutContinuation
candidates.quote: Bar 9 had formed a double top bear flag with bar 3, and its failure on the rally up from bar 16 also contributed to the bull breakout.
candidates.description: When a double-top bear-flag level is broken to the upside (the double top fails), treat the resulting breakout as reinforced and more likely to run, since traders who shorted the double top must cover into the move.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (confidence/context filter on an existing breakout entry)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to identify the double-top level before its failure can be tested

rejected.quote: Trends in many stocks are very respectful of the moving average, which means that the moving average provides opportunities all day long to enter in the direction of the trend with limited risk.
rejected.reason: asset-class generalization about stocks vs. other instruments, not a bar-level condition

chapter_summary: Short chapter restating and illustrating the trilogy-wide two-legged-move tendency (any trend, pullback, or trading-range move tends to complete in two legs, and each leg tends to subdivide into two smaller legs), plus a caution against mistaking subdivisions of a single leg for a completed two-legged correction when they sit in a tight channel and are short relative to the pattern being corrected. All of this rests on the same undefined 'leg' concept as trends chapters 19/20 and this book's own chapter 17 (research-grade, by design); this file's contribution is a concrete bar-count-fraction reading of the subdivision caution (R16-02) plus two hard-graded, more specific candidates (a measured-move target off a near-perfect breakout test, and a failed-double-top confidence boost) drawn from the chapter's worked examples. Expect the dedup pass to merge R16-01 with the existing PullbackLegCounter/LegDefinition primitives.
